This section explains the `Azure Management Hierarchy`, which defines the scopes where access control, policy, and governance are applied.

Understanding these levels is essential for scaling an Azure environment without losing control.

### *The Azure Hierarchy Of Scopes*

Azure uses a nested parent-child structure.

Decisions made at a higher level are inherited by the levels below.

<Steps>
1. `Management Groups`
2. `Subscriptions`
3. `Resource Groups`
4. `Resources`
</Steps>

### *Management Groups*

If an organization has many subscriptions, `Management Groups` provide a governance layer above the subscription level.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Scale" icon="document">
    Supports up to `10,000` management groups in a single directory.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Hierarchy" icon="setting">
    Can be nested up to `6` levels deep, in addition to the root and subscription levels.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Use Case" icon="warning">
    Apply policies such as regional restrictions or security requirements across many subscriptions at once.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Subscriptions*

A `Subscription` is a logical unit of Azure services linked to an Azure account.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Billing Boundary" icon="document">
    Invoices are generated at the subscription level.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Quota Boundary" icon="database">
    Azure service limits, such as CPU core quotas, are usually applied per subscription.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Use Case" icon="warning">
    Separate `Production` and `Development` environments so cost tracking and quotas remain isolated.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Resource Groups*

A `Resource Group` is a container for related resources that belong to the same Azure solution.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Lifecycle Boundary" icon="warning">
    Resources in the same group often share the same lifecycle. Deleting the group deletes everything inside it.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Deployment Boundary" icon="setting">
    `ARM` templates and `Bicep` deployments are usually targeted at a specific resource group.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Note" icon="document">
    A resource can belong to only one resource group, even though resources in the same group may exist in different regions.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

`Resources` are the lowest level in the hierarchy.

These are the individual Azure services you create, such as:

- `Virtual Machines`
- `Storage Accounts`
- `SQL Databases`
- `Virtual Networks`

You can apply `RBAC` directly at the resource level when very granular access is needed.

### *Scope Inheritance*

Inheritance is one of the most important concepts in Azure governance.

If a role or policy is assigned at a higher scope, it automatically applies to all child scopes below it.

<Aside type="note">
A permission assigned high in the hierarchy creates a wider blast radius because it affects more resources through inheritance.
</Aside>

### *Blast Radius Comparison*

| Scope Level | Impact Of A Change | Recommended Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Management Group | Huge | Corporate-wide policies, centralized security controls |
| Subscription | High | Billing owners, environment-wide administrators |
| Resource Group | Medium | Project teams, application contributors |
| Resource | Low | Just-in-time access, specialized tasks |

### *How To Think About Scope*

<Steps>
1. Start at the highest scope only when the rule should apply broadly.
2. Use subscription scope for environment-wide control.
3. Use resource group scope for application ownership.
4. Use resource scope only when access must be very specific.
</Steps>

This section defines the `Azure Subscription`, which acts as the main logical container for provisioning resources, controlling costs, and setting administrative boundaries.

### *The Azure Subscription*

A `Subscription` is a grouping of Azure resource categories linked to an Azure account.

It has two main roles:

- billing boundary
- access control boundary

### *The Two Primary Roles Of A Subscription*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Billing Boundary" icon="document">
    Azure usage is measured and charged at the subscription level. Each subscription generates its own billing reports and invoices.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Access Control Boundary" icon="setting">
    `RBAC` is often assigned at the subscription level, and permissions inherited here apply to all resource groups and resources inside that subscription.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

<Aside type="note">
Organizations often use multiple subscriptions to separate costs, teams, environments, or governance models.
</Aside>

### *Common Subscription Types*

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Free Account | Small credit for `30` days and a limited set of free services |
| Pay-As-You-Go | Monthly billing based on actual resource consumption |
| Enterprise Agreement | Long-term enterprise contract with committed spend and discounted pricing |
| Microsoft Customer Agreement | Modern Microsoft commerce model with streamlined billing |
| Student / Visual Studio | Monthly credits for learning and development |

### *Subscription Limits*

Each subscription has limits and quotas to avoid accidental overspending or resource exhaustion.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Default Limits" icon="warning">
    Azure applies default quotas, such as limits on the number of VMs or vCPUs that can be used in a region.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Soft Limits" icon="document">
    Many quotas are not fixed forever and can be increased if the workload requires it.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Quota Increase" icon="setting">
    If a limit is reached, a support request can be opened in the Azure Portal to request a higher quota.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Subscription Management Strategies*

When designing a large-scale environment, subscriptions are often distributed by purpose.

| Strategy | Logic | Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workload-based | Separate `Production`, `Dev`, and `Test` | Reduces blast radius between environments |
| Department-based | Separate subscriptions for `HR`, `Finance`, `IT` | Simplifies chargeback and accounting |
| Geographic-based | Separate subscriptions for `Europe`, `North America` | Helps with data residency and local compliance |

### *Moving And Transferring Subscriptions*

There are different ways to move ownership or scope in Azure.

<Steps>
1. `Resource Move`: resources can be moved between subscriptions if they are in the same tenant.
2. `Transfer of Ownership`: billing responsibility is transferred from one account to another.
3. `Tenant Change`: a subscription can move to another `Entra ID` tenant, but this is more complex and may break existing `RBAC` assignments.
</Steps>

### *Summary*

- A `Subscription` is both a billing and access boundary
- `RBAC` assigned at this level affects everything below it
- Quotas apply per subscription and are often soft limits
- Multiple subscriptions improve governance, cost control, and isolation

This section explains how to monitor, control, and optimize cloud spending with `Microsoft Cost Management + Billing`.

In Azure, costs can scale as quickly as infrastructure, so financial guardrails are as important as technical architecture.

### *Microsoft Cost Management + Billing*

This toolset helps teams move from a reactive billing mindset to a more proactive `FinOps` approach.

### *Cost Analysis*

`Cost Analysis` is the main tool for exploring spending patterns and understanding where money is going.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Granularity" icon="document">
    View costs by subscription, resource group, service name, or region.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Tagging" icon="setting">
    Use tags such as `CostCenter: Marketing` or `Project: Alpha` to attribute spend to business units or workloads.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Forecasting" icon="warning">
    Azure uses historical data to estimate spend for the next `30` to `90` days.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Budgets And Alerts*

Budgets help detect cost spikes before the end of the month.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Threshold Alerts" icon="document">
    Send notifications when spending reaches defined levels such as `50%`, `80%`, or `100%` of budget.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Anomaly Detection" icon="warning">
    Azure can flag unusual spending spikes, such as automation mistakes or unexpected usage growth.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Action Groups" icon="setting">
    Budget events can trigger automation, such as shutting down a `Dev/Test` environment when limits are exceeded.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Optimization Strategies*

Azure provides multiple ways to reduce cost without reducing value.

| Strategy | How It Works | Potential Savings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Azure Advisor | Detects idle VMs, orphaned disks, and right-sizing opportunities | `15% - 25%` |
| Reservations | Commit to `1` or `3` years for specific resources | Up to `72%` |
| Savings Plans | Commit to a fixed hourly spend across compute services | Up to `65%` |
| Spot Instances | Use excess Azure capacity for interruptible workloads | Up to `90%` |
| Hybrid Benefit | Reuse existing Windows or SQL Server licenses | Up to `40%` |

### *Billing Vs. Cost Management*

Although they are related, they serve different roles.

| Area | Focus | Typical User |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing | Payment methods, invoices, tax documents | Finance teams |
| Cost Management | Usage tracking, optimization, daily cost control | Engineers and architects |

### *2026 Focus: FinOps For AI*

With the growth of `Azure OpenAI` and `Microsoft Fabric`, cost management now also requires close monitoring of AI-related usage.

Examples include:

- token consumption
- model usage
- AI capacity units

<Aside type="note">
High-cost AI services should be isolated into dedicated resource groups so their usage can be monitored more clearly.
</Aside>

### *Practical Cost Review Flow*

<Steps>
1. Use `Cost Analysis` to identify where spending is increasing.
2. Apply tags to improve attribution by project, team, or environment.
3. Set budgets and alerts before overspending happens.
4. Review optimization recommendations such as reservations or idle resource cleanup.
5. Isolate expensive workloads, especially AI services, for easier monitoring.
</Steps>

### *Key Rule*

<Aside type="caution">
Always delete orphaned disks. If a VM is deleted but its disk is kept, Azure continues charging for the disk.
</Aside>

This section covers `Azure Virtual Machines`, the core `Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)` offering for running scalable compute resources in the cloud.

### *Azure Virtual Machines*

An Azure `VM` gives you the flexibility of virtualization without owning the physical hardware.

You are responsible for:

- configuring the operating system
- patching the system
- maintaining installed software

### *VM Size Families*

Azure groups VMs into `families`, also called `series`, optimized for different workloads.

Choosing the right series is one of the most important decisions for balancing performance and cost.

| Family | Series Examples | Best Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General Purpose | `B`, `D-Series` | Testing, small databases, balanced web servers |
| Compute Optimized | `F-Series` | High-traffic web servers, batch processing, game servers |
| Memory Optimized | `E`, `M-Series` | SQL, Oracle, SAP HANA, in-memory analytics |
| Storage Optimized | `L-Series` | NoSQL databases and data warehousing |
| GPU / Accelerated | `N-Series` | AI training, rendering, video processing |
| High Performance Compute | `H-Series` | Scientific workloads such as weather modeling |

<Aside type="note">
As of `2026`, newer processors such as `Cobalt 100` and `Intel Xeon 6` are widely available in `D` and `E` series, improving price-to-performance compared to older generations.
</Aside>

### *Storage And Disks*

Every VM includes at least:

- an `OS Disk`
- a `Temporary Disk`

The temporary disk is usually exposed as `D:` and its data is lost when the VM is deallocated.

For persistent application data, additional `Data Disks` must be attached.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Standard HDD" icon="document">
    Best for backup, archives, and infrequent access workloads.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Standard SSD" icon="setting">
    Good for light workloads that need more consistency than HDD.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Premium SSD" icon="warning">
    High-performance low-latency storage and required for the `99.9%` single-instance SLA.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Ultra Disk" icon="rocket">
    Designed for extremely demanding databases that require very high IOPS and very low latency.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Availability Options*

Azure provides different placement strategies to reduce downtime.

| Option | Purpose | SLA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single VM | No redundancy | `99.9%` with Premium SSD |
| Availability Sets | Protect against hardware failure in one datacenter | `99.95%` |
| Availability Zones | Protect against full datacenter failure | `99.99%` |
| VM Scale Sets | Automatically deploy and scale identical VMs | Depends on design |

### *Virtual Machine Scale Sets*

`Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS)` automatically create and manage a group of identical VMs.

They are useful when an application must:

- scale out automatically
- distribute traffic
- maintain consistent configuration across many instances

### *Lifecycle And Cost Management*

VM billing depends on the runtime state.

<Steps>
1. A VM in the `Running` state is billed by the second.
2. If the VM is shut down only from inside the operating system, it may remain in the `Stopped` state and still incur charges.
3. To stop billing for compute, the VM must reach the `Deallocated` state.
4. This is usually done by stopping the VM from the Azure Portal, CLI, or automation.
</Steps>

### *Spot Instances*

`Spot Instances` use unused Azure capacity at a large discount.

They can save up to `90%`, but Azure may evict the VM with short notice if capacity is needed elsewhere.

They are best suited for:

- batch jobs
- CI/CD agents
- interruptible workloads

### *Management Best Practices*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Azure Bastion" icon="warning">
    Avoid exposing `RDP` or `SSH` directly to the public internet. Use `Azure Bastion` for secure browser-based access.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Auto-Shutdown" icon="setting">
    For `Dev/Test` environments, enable scheduled shutdown to reduce unnecessary compute costs.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Extensions" icon="document">
    Use VM Extensions to automatically install monitoring agents, antivirus, or configuration tools during deployment.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

This section explains `Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets`, the main Azure service for building highly available and auto-scaling VM fleets.

### *Virtual Machine Scale Sets*

A standard `Virtual Machine` is a single server.

A `Scale Set` is a group of identical, load-balanced VMs designed to be managed as a pool instead of as individual machines.

<Aside type="note">
`VMSS` is commonly used for stateless application tiers that must scale automatically as traffic changes.
</Aside>

### *Key Features*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Auto-Scaling" icon="setting">
    Automatically increases or decreases the number of VM instances based on CPU, memory, or time-based schedules.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Load Balancing" icon="document">
    Integrates with `Azure Load Balancer` or `Application Gateway` to distribute traffic across instances.
  </Card>

  <Card title="High Availability" icon="warning">
    Spreads instances across fault domains or availability zones to reduce downtime during failures.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Uniform Configuration" icon="database">
    New VMs are created from the same base image and configuration so scale-out instances remain consistent.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Orchestration Modes*

In `2026`, Azure provides two orchestration models for a scale set.

| Mode | Description | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uniform | Uses one template model and keeps all instances identical | Large stateless workloads such as web tiers |
| Flexible | Allows different VM sizes and more individual control | Stateful workloads or mixed Spot and on-demand usage |

### *Scaling Mechanics*

Scaling defines how the VM fleet grows or shrinks.

<Steps>
1. `Scale Out`: more VMs are added when demand increases.
2. `Scale In`: VMs are removed when traffic drops.
3. `Overprovisioning`: Azure may create extra instances temporarily so failed startup attempts do not prevent reaching the target capacity.
</Steps>

### *Upgrade Policies*

When the scale set image is updated, Azure can roll out the change in different ways.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Manual" icon="document">
    Updates are applied only when the administrator chooses each instance.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Automatic" icon="setting">
    Azure updates instances in controlled batches while keeping part of the fleet online.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Rolling" icon="warning">
    Azure updates instances progressively in waves and checks health between each wave.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Why Use VMSS Instead Of Individual VMs*

| Benefit | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Management At Scale | Updating or scaling a large fleet is handled from one central definition |
| Cost Efficiency | You only pay for the instances currently running |
| Redundancy | If one VM fails, the scale set can automatically replace it |

### *Typical Flow*

<Steps>
1. Define the base image and VM configuration.
2. Attach the scale set to a load balancer or application gateway.
3. Configure scaling rules based on demand.
4. Azure adds or removes VM instances automatically.
5. Failed instances are replaced to maintain capacity.
</Steps>

This section covers `Azure App Service`, the main `Platform as a Service (PaaS)` offering for hosting web applications, APIs, and background workloads without managing virtual machines directly.

### *Azure App Service*

`Azure App Service` allows you to deploy and run applications without managing the underlying operating system, patching, or server infrastructure.

It is commonly used for:

- web applications
- REST APIs
- backend services
- scheduled or background jobs

<Aside type="note">
With App Service, Azure manages the platform while you focus on the application code and runtime configuration.
</Aside>

### *Supported Workloads*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Web Apps" icon="document">
    Host websites and frontend applications with built-in scaling, TLS, and deployment support.
  </Card>

  <Card title="API Apps" icon="setting">
    Run backend APIs with authentication, routing, and monitoring integration.
  </Card>

  <Card title="WebJobs" icon="warning">
    Execute scheduled or background tasks alongside an App Service application.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Key Features*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Auto-Scaling" icon="setting">
    Increase or decrease the number of instances based on traffic, CPU usage, or schedules.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Custom Domains & TLS" icon="document">
    Bind custom domains and secure them with managed or uploaded certificates.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Deployment Slots" icon="database">
    Deploy a staging version of the app and swap it into production with reduced risk.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Built-In Monitoring" icon="warning">
    Integrates with `Azure Monitor` and `Application Insights` for logs, metrics, and diagnostics.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *App Service Plan*

An `App Service Plan` defines the compute resources used by one or more App Service apps.

It controls:

- pricing tier
- region
- instance size
- scaling limits

Multiple apps can share the same plan, which means they also share the underlying compute resources.

### *Pricing Tiers*

| Tier | Typical Use |
| --- | --- |
| Free / Shared | Learning, testing, small demos |
| Basic | Small production workloads with dedicated resources |
| Standard | Production apps needing scaling and staging slots |
| Premium | High-performance workloads, advanced scaling, networking features |
| Isolated | Highly secure workloads running in dedicated environments |

### *Deployment Flow*

<Steps>
1. Create or choose an `App Service Plan`.
2. Create the `Web App` or `API App`.
3. Deploy the application code using Git, ZIP deploy, CI/CD, or container images.
4. Configure environment variables, connection strings, and custom domains.
5. Scale the app horizontally or vertically as traffic changes.
</Steps>

### *Deployment Slots*

`Deployment Slots` let you run multiple versions of the same app inside the same App Service.

Common example:

- `staging`
- `production`

This allows you to:

- validate a release before exposing it to users
- perform safer production swaps
- reduce downtime during releases

### *Scaling Options*

| Scaling Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Scale Up | Increase CPU, memory, and instance size |
| Scale Out | Add more app instances |
| Scheduled Scaling | Change capacity based on time of day |
| Metric-Based Scaling | Scale automatically using metrics such as CPU or request count |

### *Best Practices*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Use Deployment Slots" icon="document">
    Test releases in staging before swapping to production.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Store Secrets Safely" icon="warning">
    Use `Azure Key Vault` or App Settings instead of hardcoding secrets in the application.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Enable Monitoring" icon="setting">
    Connect the app to `Application Insights` for observability and troubleshooting.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Choose The Right Plan" icon="database">
    Avoid overpaying by matching the App Service tier to the workload profile.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

This section covers `Azure Container Instances`, the fastest and simplest way to run containers in Azure without managing servers or orchestrators.

### *Azure Container Instances*

If a `Virtual Machine` is a house and a `Scale Set` is a housing development, `Azure Container Instances (ACI)` is like a hotel room.

You start it when needed, use it for a short time, and stop paying when it is no longer required.

`ACI` is a serverless container service.

You provide a container image, and Azure runs it without requiring VM management or a Kubernetes cluster.

<Aside type="note">
`ACI` is ideal when you need containers quickly but do not want the operational overhead of managing infrastructure.
</Aside>

### *Why ACI Is Considered Serverless*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Zero Infrastructure Management" icon="document">
    You do not manage the underlying VM, operating system, patching, or physical hardware.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Rapid Startup" icon="setting">
    Containers can start in seconds, which is much faster than most virtual machine startup times.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Per-Second Billing" icon="warning">
    Billing is based on the `vCPU` and memory consumed, calculated down to the second.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Container Groups*

The top-level ACI resource is a `Container Group`.

A container group is a collection of containers scheduled on the same host machine.

Containers inside the same group share:

- lifecycle
- local network
- mounted storage volumes

This makes ACI useful for the `sidecar pattern`, where one container runs the main application and another handles tasks such as logging or synchronization.

### *How ACI Works*

<Steps>
1. You provide a container image, usually from a container registry.
2. Azure creates a `Container Group`.
3. The containers start on shared infrastructure managed by Microsoft.
4. The workload runs for as long as needed.
5. When the workload finishes, the container group can stop and billing ends.
</Steps>

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="CI/CD Build Agents" icon="document">
    A container starts during a pipeline run, builds the application, executes tests, and then shuts down.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Data Processing" icon="database">
    A file event triggers a container to start, process data, write results, and exit.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Bursting From Kubernetes" icon="warning">
    `AKS` can temporarily offload extra work into `ACI` when demand spikes.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *When To Use ACI*

| Good Fit | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Short-lived workloads | Fast startup and per-second billing |
| Simple container execution | No cluster or VM management required |
| Event-driven jobs | Containers can run only when triggered |
| Temporary burst capacity | Useful for handling short demand peaks |

### *Summary*

- `ACI` is the simplest Azure service for running containers
- It is a `serverless container` platform
- `Container Groups` allow multiple containers to share lifecycle and networking
- It works well for temporary, event-driven, and burst workloads

This section covers `Azure Container Apps`, a serverless container platform designed for modern applications and microservices.

### *Azure Container Apps*

If `ACI` is a hotel room for a short stay, `Azure Container Apps (ACA)` is a serviced apartment.

It is still serverless, but it includes built-in features that make it suitable for running full applications and microservices.

`ACA` is built on top of `Kubernetes`, but Microsoft hides most of the cluster management and operational complexity.

This makes it a middle ground between:

- very simple `ACI`
- more advanced and fully managed `AKS`

<Aside type="note">
`Azure Container Apps` gives you many Kubernetes-style capabilities without requiring you to manage a Kubernetes cluster directly.
</Aside>

### *Why Use Azure Container Apps*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Scale To Zero" icon="document">
    If the application receives no traffic, it can scale down to `0` running replicas to reduce cost.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Automatic Ingress" icon="setting">
    Azure handles HTTPS exposure, certificates, and routing for public application access.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Microservice Friendly" icon="database">
    Built-in support for `Dapr` helps services communicate, manage state, and work with pub/sub patterns.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *How ACA Fits In Azure Compute*

`ACA` fills the gap between simpler container execution and full cluster orchestration.

| Service | Best For |
| --- | --- |
| `ACI` | Short-lived, simple containers |
| `ACA` | Microservices, APIs, event-driven apps |
| `AKS` | Full Kubernetes control and advanced orchestration |

### *KEDA-Based Scaling*

Unlike `VM Scale Sets`, which usually scale on CPU or memory, `ACA` uses `KEDA` (`Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling`).

This allows scaling based on richer signals.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="HTTP Traffic" icon="document">
    Scale up when request concurrency reaches a defined level, such as more than `50` concurrent requests.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Message Queues" icon="warning">
    Scale up when queue depth increases, such as when more than `100` messages are waiting in `Azure Service Bus`.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Events" icon="setting">
    Scale based on external event sources such as `Kafka`, `RabbitMQ`, or even SQL-driven triggers.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Deployment Features*

`Azure Container Apps` supports modern release strategies for safer deployments.

- rolling updates
- blue/green deployments
- canary deployments

### *Typical Flow*

<Steps>
1. Deploy a container image to `Azure Container Apps`.
2. Configure ingress, environment variables, and scaling rules.
3. Azure exposes the app over HTTPS.
4. `KEDA` scales replicas based on traffic or events.
5. If no traffic exists, the app can scale down to `0`.
</Steps>

### *Summary*

- `ACA` is a serverless platform for containerized applications
- It is built on Kubernetes, but the cluster is hidden from the user
- It is ideal for microservices and event-driven workloads
- `KEDA` enables more advanced autoscaling than basic CPU or memory rules

This section introduces `Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)`, the most powerful and flexible Azure platform for running containers at scale.

### *Azure Kubernetes Service*

If `ACA` is a managed apartment, `AKS` is a custom-built skyscraper.

`AKS` is Azure's managed Kubernetes offering. Microsoft manages the Kubernetes control plane, while you manage the worker nodes where applications run.

<Aside type="note">
`AKS` gives full Kubernetes capabilities, but also requires more design, operations, and governance effort than `ACI` or `ACA`.
</Aside>

### *Core Architecture*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Control Plane" icon="document">
    Managed by Azure and includes the API server, scheduler, and `etcd`. It is free unless the uptime SLA tier is enabled.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Worker Nodes" icon="database">
    Azure virtual machines where your workloads run. You choose the VM size, node count, and scaling model.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Node Pools*

Instead of managing one flat list of VMs, `AKS` organizes nodes into `node pools`.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="System Pools" icon="setting">
    Reserved for core Kubernetes services such as DNS, networking, and cluster infrastructure components.
  </Card>

  <Card title="User Pools" icon="warning">
    Used for application workloads. Multiple pools can be created for different workload types such as GPU nodes or Spot nodes.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Pods, Not Containers*

In Kubernetes, workloads are deployed as `Pods`, not as standalone containers.

A pod is a wrapper around one or more containers that share:

- network
- storage
- lifecycle context

### *Why Choose AKS*

The main reason to choose `AKS` over `ACA` is control.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Full Kubernetes API" icon="document">
    Standard Kubernetes tools such as `Helm`, `Prometheus`, and `Istio` work on AKS.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Advanced Networking" icon="setting">
    You can choose between `Kubenet` and `Azure CNI`, depending on IP management and network integration needs.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Hybrid Cloud" icon="warning">
    With `Azure Arc`, Kubernetes clusters running on-premises or in other clouds can be managed from Azure.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Scaling In AKS*

AKS supports scaling at multiple levels.

| Scaling Layer | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `HPA` | Adds more pods when demand increases |
| `VPA` | Adjusts pod CPU and memory requests |
| `Cluster Autoscaler` | Adds more nodes when the cluster runs out of capacity |

### *AKS Workflow*

<Steps>
1. Azure creates and manages the Kubernetes control plane.
2. You define one or more node pools for workloads.
3. Applications are deployed as pods.
4. Kubernetes schedules pods onto available nodes.
5. AKS can scale pods and nodes as demand changes.
</Steps>

### *Summary*

- `AKS` is Azure's managed Kubernetes platform
- Azure manages the control plane, while you manage worker nodes
- `Node Pools` separate system workloads from application workloads
- AKS is chosen when full Kubernetes control is required

This section explains the networking and identity models behind `Azure Kubernetes Service`.

These are two of the most important design areas in any AKS architecture.

### *AKS Networking Models*

There are two main networking approaches in AKS.

| Model | Description | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Azure CNI` | Every pod gets an IP from the Azure virtual network | Best integration, but consumes more IP addresses |
| `Kubenet` | Pods use a private internal IP range | Saves VNet IP space, but adds routing complexity |

### *Azure CNI*

`Azure CNI` gives each pod a real IP address from the Azure virtual network.

Benefits:

- direct Azure network integration
- strong performance
- simpler communication between pods and other Azure resources

Tradeoff:

- pod IPs consume subnet space
- a small subnet can fill up quickly

<Aside type="note">
Many teams now prefer `Azure CNI Overlay`, which reduces subnet pressure while keeping good Azure network integration.
</Aside>

### *Kubenet*

`Kubenet` gives pods IPs from a private internal range that Azure does not directly manage.

Benefits:

- saves VNet IP addresses
- only one VNet IP is consumed per node

Tradeoff:

- relies on user-defined routes
- adds more complexity and some latency

### *Identity In AKS*

Identity in AKS is split into two layers.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Cluster Access" icon="document">
    Human users access the cluster through `Microsoft Entra ID` instead of shared admin credentials.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Workload Identity" icon="setting">
    Applications inside pods access Azure resources by using federated managed identities instead of secrets.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Cluster Access*

For user access, AKS can be integrated with `Microsoft Entra ID`.

This allows:

- login with corporate accounts
- MFA enforcement
- role assignment through Entra groups
- immediate access removal when an account is disabled

Typical roles include:

- `AKS Cluster Admin`
- `AKS Cluster User`

### *Workload Identity*

`Workload Identity` allows a pod to access Azure services without storing passwords or connection strings.

This is commonly used when an application in AKS needs access to:

- `Azure Storage`
- `Key Vault`
- databases
- messaging services

### *Security Chain*

To understand workload identity, it helps to see the chain from organizational identity down to pod identity.

| Component | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `Tenant` | Microsoft Entra ID instance for the organization |
| `Subscription` | Billing and quota boundary linked to the tenant |
| `Managed Identity` | Azure-managed identity linked to a resource |
| `Service Account` | Kubernetes-native identity used by pods |

### *How Workload Identity Works*

<Steps>
1. A `User-Assigned Managed Identity` is created in Azure.
2. A `Service Account` is created inside the AKS cluster.
3. Azure is configured to trust that service account from that specific AKS cluster.
4. A pod runs using that service account.
5. Azure exchanges that trust relationship for a token tied to the managed identity.
6. The pod uses the token to access Azure services securely.
</Steps>

### *Summary*

- `Azure CNI` gives pods direct VNet integration
- `Kubenet` saves IP space but adds routing complexity
- `Cluster Access` secures human access through Entra ID
- `Workload Identity` secures application access without secrets

This section covers `Azure Key Vault`, the central Azure service for storing and protecting sensitive information.

### *Azure Key Vault*

`Azure Key Vault` is the secure location for storing sensitive digital assets such as passwords, API keys, and certificates.

In modern cloud architecture, secrets should not be hard-coded into source code or configuration files.

Instead, applications should retrieve them from `Key Vault` at runtime.

<Aside type="note">
`Key Vault` is a foundational security service in Azure and is commonly used together with managed identities to avoid storing credentials in applications.
</Aside>

### *Object Types In Key Vault*

`Azure Key Vault` stores three main types of objects.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Secrets" icon="document">
    Plain values such as passwords, connection strings, or API keys that can be written and read as text.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Keys" icon="setting">
    Cryptographic keys used for encryption and decryption. The private key material is normally not exposed directly.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Certificates" icon="warning">
    SSL and TLS certificates used for secure communication. Key Vault can also help manage renewal.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Key Protection Tiers*

When creating a vault, you choose the protection level for stored keys.

| Tier | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Standard | Uses software-protected keys with strong security at lower cost |
| Premium | Uses `HSM`-backed protection with dedicated hardware security modules |

`Premium` is used when stronger cryptographic protection or regulatory requirements make `HSM` support necessary.

### *Access Models*

There are two ways to control access to a vault.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Azure RBAC" icon="setting">
    Recommended model. Uses Azure role assignments such as `Key Vault Secrets User` at the vault scope.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Access Policies" icon="warning">
    Legacy model. Uses a separate permission list inside the vault to manually allow operations such as `Get`, `List`, or `Delete`.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

<Aside type="note">
`Azure RBAC` is generally the preferred and more modern model because it aligns Key Vault access with the rest of Azure governance.
</Aside>

### *How Applications Use Key Vault*

Applications usually access Key Vault through a managed identity instead of through stored credentials.

<Steps>
1. The application is assigned a `Managed Identity`.
2. That identity is granted access to the vault using `Azure RBAC`.
3. The application requests a token from Azure.
4. The token is used to access secrets, keys, or certificates in `Key Vault`.
5. The secret is retrieved securely at runtime.
</Steps>

### *Key Vault In Kubernetes*

In Kubernetes environments, the `Secrets Store CSI Driver` can connect a cluster to external secret providers such as `Azure Key Vault`.

Its role is to:

- fetch secrets from Key Vault
- mount them into the pod as files
- avoid storing sensitive values directly in manifests

This lets an application read secrets from the file system instead of embedding them in the container image or deployment YAML.

### *Why Key Vault Matters*

| Benefit | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Centralization | Sensitive values are stored in one secure service |
| Rotation | Secrets and certificates can be updated without changing application code |
| Reduced Exposure | Applications do not need hard-coded credentials |
| Integration | Works with managed identities, RBAC, and Kubernetes secret providers |

### *Summary*

- `Key Vault` stores secrets, cryptographic keys, and certificates
- `Standard` and `Premium` tiers define the strength of key protection
- `Azure RBAC` is the recommended access model
- Applications should use managed identities to access Key Vault securely
- In Kubernetes, the `Secrets Store CSI Driver` can mount Key Vault secrets into pods

This section covers `Azure Virtual Network`, the core networking service used to build private connectivity in Azure.

### *Virtual Network*

A `Virtual Network (VNet)` is a logically isolated private network in Azure.

It acts as your own network sandbox where you define private IP address ranges, such as `10.0.0.0/16`.

Inside a VNet, resources can communicate privately and can be segmented according to function or security needs.

<Aside type="note">
A `VNet` is the foundation for most Azure networking designs, including subnets, private workloads, hybrid connectivity, and hub-and-spoke architectures.
</Aside>

### *Subnets*

`Subnets` are smaller network segments inside a `VNet`.

They are used to organize resources and apply different security boundaries.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Public Subnet" icon="document">
    Typically used for resources such as web servers that need connectivity to the internet.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Private Subnet" icon="warning">
    Used for internal services such as databases that should not be directly reachable from the internet.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Gateway Subnet" icon="setting">
    Reserved subnet required for services such as `VPN Gateway` when connecting Azure to on-premises environments.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *VNet Peering*

By default, two different `VNets` cannot communicate.

`VNet Peering` creates a private connection between them.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Low Latency" icon="document">
    Peered traffic stays on Microsoft's private global network and does not traverse the public internet.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Regional Or Global" icon="setting">
    VNets can be peered within the same region or across different regions.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Non-Transitive" icon="warning">
    If `VNet A` is peered with `VNet B`, and `VNet B` is peered with `VNet C`, then `VNet A` cannot automatically talk to `VNet C`.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>


### *Hybrid Connectivity Options*

When Azure must communicate with physical infrastructure on-premises, there are three main connectivity models.

| Option | Description | Typical Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Point-to-Site VPN | One computer connects to Azure through an encrypted tunnel | Remote developers, small environments |
| Site-to-Site VPN | An entire office network connects to Azure through a permanent encrypted tunnel over the internet | Small and medium businesses |
| ExpressRoute | Dedicated private connection between the datacenter and Azure | Large enterprises with high bandwidth and low latency requirements |

### *Hub And Spoke Architecture*

A common Azure networking design is the `Hub and Spoke` model.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Hub" icon="document">
    Central VNet containing shared services such as firewalls, VPN gateways, or ExpressRoute gateways.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Spokes" icon="database">
    Separate VNets used by individual applications, teams, or projects.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Connection" icon="setting">
    Each spoke is peered to the hub so workloads can share common connectivity and security services.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>


### *Typical Flow*

<Steps>
1. Create a `Virtual Network` with a defined address space.
2. Divide the VNet into subnets based on workload type and security needs.
3. Peer VNets together when separate environments must communicate.
4. Add hybrid connectivity with `VPN` or `ExpressRoute` if on-premises access is required.
5. Use a `Hub and Spoke` design when multiple projects must share central networking services.
</Steps>


### *Summary*

- `VNet` is the private networking foundation of Azure
- `Subnets` organize and isolate workloads
- `VNet Peering` connects VNets privately but is not transitive
- `VPN` and `ExpressRoute` connect Azure to on-premises networks
- `Hub and Spoke` is a common enterprise design for shared connectivity and security

This section covers `Network Security Groups`, the main Azure service used to filter traffic inside a virtual network.

### *Network Security Groups*

A `Network Security Group (NSG)` is a basic stateful firewall that filters traffic at the network and transport layers, corresponding to `OSI Layer 3` and `Layer 4`.

It is the main tool used to enforce micro-segmentation inside a `Virtual Network`.

You can think of an `NSG` as a list of access control rules that decide which packets are allowed and which are blocked.

<Aside type="note">
`NSGs` are commonly used to control east-west traffic inside a VNet and to protect workloads from unnecessary exposure.
</Aside>

### *Where To Associate An NSG*

An `NSG` can be attached in two places.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Subnet Level" icon="document">
    Recommended in most cases. One NSG protects all resources inside the subnet and is easier to manage consistently.
  </Card>

  <Card title="NIC Level" icon="warning">
    Attached directly to a specific virtual machine network interface. Usually used only when one VM needs special rules.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *How NSG Rules Work*

Each NSG rule is defined by a `5-tuple`.

- source
- destination
- source port
- destination port
- protocol

Rules are processed by priority, from `100` to `4096`.

Lower numbers have higher priority.

As soon as traffic matches a rule, Azure stops evaluating the rest and applies that action.

<Aside type="note">
It is a good practice to leave gaps between rule priorities, such as `100`, `110`, and `120`, so new rules can be added later without renumbering everything.
</Aside>

### *Default Rules*

Every NSG includes some default rules.

| Rule | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `AllowVNetInBound` | Allows communication between resources in the same VNet |
| `AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound` | Allows Azure load balancer health probes |
| `DenyAllInBound` | Blocks inbound traffic that does not match any earlier rule |

### *Service Tags And ASGs*

Managing individual IP addresses at scale is difficult, so Azure provides abstractions to simplify rule definitions.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Service Tags" icon="setting">
    Use predefined Azure service names such as `AzureKeyVault` instead of maintaining IP address ranges manually.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Application Security Groups" icon="database">
    Group VMs by function instead of by IP address, such as `Web-Servers` or `App-Servers`.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Example With ASGs*

Instead of writing rules for ten separate VM IP addresses, you can place all web servers into an `ASG` named `Web-Servers`.

The NSG rule can then say:

- allow traffic from the internet
- to `Web-Servers`
- on port `80`

This makes the rules easier to read and easier to maintain.


### *Typical Evaluation Flow*

<Steps>
1. Traffic reaches a subnet or network interface protected by an `NSG`.
2. Azure evaluates rules from the lowest priority number to the highest.
3. The first matching rule is applied.
4. If no custom rule matches, Azure continues to the default rules.
5. If nothing allows the traffic, it is denied.
</Steps>

### *Summary*

- `NSG` is a stateful Layer 3 and Layer 4 firewall
- It can be attached to a subnet or directly to a NIC
- Rules are processed by priority and stop at the first match
- `Service Tags` simplify Azure service targeting
- `ASGs` simplify rules by grouping workloads by role instead of IP

This section covers `Azure Firewall`, the managed Azure service used to centrally inspect and control network traffic.

### *Azure Firewall*

`Azure Firewall` is a managed, cloud-native `Firewall as a Service (FWaaS)`.

It is `stateful`, which means it understands the full conversation between endpoints rather than inspecting packets in isolation.

`Azure Firewall` is commonly used when organizations need centralized inbound and outbound traffic control across multiple virtual networks.

<Aside type="note">
Unlike `NSGs`, which are usually applied close to individual workloads, `Azure Firewall` is typically deployed as a shared inspection point in a hub network.
</Aside>

### *Firewall SKUs*

Azure Firewall is available in three main SKUs.

| SKU | Typical Use | Main Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic | Small projects and simpler environments | Essential Layer 3-7 filtering |
| Standard | Enterprise production workloads | Layer 3-7 filtering with threat intelligence |
| Premium | High-security and regulated environments | Adds advanced inspection such as `IDPS` and `TLS Inspection` |

### *Premium Features*

The `Premium` tier includes advanced security controls.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="IDPS" icon="warning">
    Intrusion Detection and Prevention System monitors traffic patterns and helps block known malicious activity.
  </Card>

  <Card title="TLS Inspection" icon="setting">
    The firewall can decrypt HTTPS traffic, inspect it, and re-encrypt it before forwarding it.
  </Card>

  <Card title="URL Filtering" icon="document">
    Filtering can be applied at a more granular URL level instead of only at the domain level.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Why Azure Firewall Is Centralized*

Deploying a separate firewall in every `VNet` is usually too expensive and harder to manage.

The common Azure pattern is `Hub and Spoke`.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Hub" icon="document">
    A central VNet hosts shared services, including `Azure Firewall`, inside a dedicated subnet named `AzureFirewallSubnet`.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Spokes" icon="database">
    Application VNets are peered to the hub instead of hosting their own firewall instances.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Routing" icon="setting">
    `User Defined Routes (UDRs)` force traffic from spoke subnets to pass through the firewall first.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Traffic Flow In Hub And Spoke*

<Steps>
1. Deploy `Azure Firewall` in the hub VNet inside `AzureFirewallSubnet`.
2. Peer application VNets to the hub.
3. Create `UDRs` in spoke subnets.
4. Route traffic such as `0.0.0.0/0` to the private IP of the firewall.
5. Let the firewall inspect and allow or deny traffic based on policy.
</Steps>

### *Firewall Vs. NSG*

| Service | Main Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `NSG` | Basic Layer 3-4 filtering close to subnets and NICs |
| `Azure Firewall` | Centralized Layer 3-7 inspection and advanced traffic control |

### *Summary*

- `Azure Firewall` is a managed and stateful firewall service
- It is available in `Basic`, `Standard`, and `Premium` tiers
- `Premium` adds `IDPS`, `TLS Inspection`, and more advanced filtering
- It is commonly deployed in a `Hub and Spoke` architecture
- `UDRs` are used to force traffic through the firewall

This section covers `Azure Load Balancer`, the Azure service used to distribute network traffic across multiple backend resources.

### *Azure Load Balancer*

`Azure Load Balancer` is a Layer 4 load balancer.

It distributes `TCP` and `UDP` traffic based on:

- source IP
- destination IP
- source port
- destination port
- protocol

It is designed for very high performance and high availability, but it does not inspect HTTP content like URLs or cookies.

<Aside type="note">
`Azure Load Balancer` works at the transport layer. If you need Layer 7 features such as SSL termination, path-based routing, or a web application firewall, `Application Gateway` is usually the better choice.
</Aside>

### *Main Load Balancer Types*

Azure Load Balancer is commonly used in two forms.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Public Load Balancer" icon="document">
    Distributes internet-facing traffic to backend resources such as virtual machines or scale sets.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Internal Load Balancer" icon="database">
    Distributes private traffic inside a virtual network or between internal applications.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *How It Works*

`Azure Load Balancer` sends traffic to healthy backend instances.

The core pieces are:

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Frontend IP" icon="document">
    The IP address that clients connect to, either public or private.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Backend Pool" icon="setting">
    The group of virtual machines, VM scale sets, or IP addresses that receive traffic.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Health Probes" icon="warning">
    Checks whether a backend instance is healthy before traffic is sent to it.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Load Balancing Rules*

A load balancer uses rules to map frontend traffic to the backend pool.

Typical examples include:

- forward frontend port `80` to backend port `80`
- forward frontend port `443` to backend port `443`

If a backend instance fails the health probe, it is removed from traffic rotation until it becomes healthy again.

### *SKU Options*

| SKU | Typical Use | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic | Small or legacy deployments | Limited features and smaller scope |
| Standard | Production workloads | More secure, more scalable, and recommended for modern deployments |

<Aside type="note">
`Standard Load Balancer` is the preferred option for production because it offers better scalability, availability, and security controls.
</Aside>

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="VM Redundancy" icon="document">
    Distribute traffic across multiple virtual machines so one server failure does not bring down the application.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Scale Sets" icon="setting">
    Balance traffic across instances in a `VM Scale Set`.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Internal Services" icon="database">
    Expose backend services privately inside a `VNet` without making them public on the internet.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Traffic Flow*

<Steps>
1. A client connects to the frontend IP of the load balancer.
2. The load balancer checks the configured rule for the destination port and protocol.
3. Healthy backend instances are identified through health probes.
4. Traffic is forwarded to one of the healthy backends.
5. If a backend fails the probe, it stops receiving traffic.
</Steps>

### *Azure Load Balancer Vs. Application Gateway*

| Service | Layer | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Azure Load Balancer` | Layer 4 | High-performance TCP and UDP traffic distribution |
| `Application Gateway` | Layer 7 | Web traffic with routing, TLS termination, and WAF support |

### *Summary*

- `Azure Load Balancer` distributes `TCP` and `UDP` traffic at Layer 4
- It can be public or internal
- It relies on frontend IPs, backend pools, rules, and health probes
- `Standard` is the recommended SKU for production
- It is commonly used with VMs and VM scale sets

This section covers `Azure Application Gateway`, the Azure service used to route and protect web traffic at the application layer.

### *Azure Application Gateway*

`Azure Application Gateway` is a Layer 7 load balancer.

Unlike `Azure Load Balancer`, which works at the transport layer, `Application Gateway` understands HTTP and HTTPS traffic.

This allows it to make routing decisions based on:

- host name
- URL path
- HTTP headers
- HTTPS configuration

<Aside type="note">
`Application Gateway` is the preferred Azure service when you need advanced web traffic handling such as TLS termination, path-based routing, or web application firewall protection.
</Aside>

### *Key Features*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Layer 7 Routing" icon="document">
    Routes web traffic based on host names and URL paths instead of only IP addresses and ports.
  </Card>

  <Card title="TLS Termination" icon="setting">
    Can handle HTTPS encryption at the gateway so backend applications do not need to manage the same TLS workload themselves.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Web Application Firewall" icon="warning">
    Optional `WAF` protection helps block common web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *How It Works*

An `Application Gateway` sits between clients and backend web applications.

Its main components include:

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Frontend Listener" icon="document">
    Accepts incoming HTTP or HTTPS traffic on a public or private IP.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Routing Rules" icon="setting">
    Decides where traffic should go based on host names, paths, or listener settings.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Backend Pool" icon="database">
    Contains the target web servers, virtual machines, scale sets, or app services.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Routing Capabilities*

`Application Gateway` supports more advanced routing than a Layer 4 load balancer.

| Feature | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Host-based routing | Send traffic to different backends based on the requested domain |
| Path-based routing | Send requests to different backends based on URL paths such as `/api` or `/images` |
| TLS termination | Decrypt HTTPS traffic at the gateway |
| End-to-end TLS | Re-encrypt traffic from the gateway to the backend if needed |

### *Web Application Firewall*

The optional `WAF` tier adds protection for web applications.

It helps detect and block common application attacks such as:

- SQL injection
- cross-site scripting
- malicious HTTP patterns

This makes it useful for internet-facing applications that must be protected at the HTTP layer.

### *Typical Flow*

<Steps>
1. A client sends an HTTP or HTTPS request to the gateway.
2. The listener accepts the request on the configured frontend IP and port.
3. Routing rules inspect the request.
4. The request is forwarded to the correct backend pool.
5. If `WAF` is enabled, the request is also inspected for malicious patterns.
</Steps>

### *Application Gateway Vs. Load Balancer*

| Service | Layer | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Azure Load Balancer` | Layer 4 | Fast `TCP` and `UDP` traffic distribution |
| `Application Gateway` | Layer 7 | Web apps needing advanced routing and optional `WAF` |

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Web Applications" icon="document">
    Route browser traffic to one or more backend web applications.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Microservices" icon="setting">
    Send traffic to different services based on host names or URL paths.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Secure Internet Entry" icon="warning">
    Protect public-facing applications with `WAF` and central TLS handling.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Summary*

- `Application Gateway` is a Layer 7 web traffic load balancer
- It understands HTTP and HTTPS traffic
- It supports host-based and path-based routing
- It can terminate TLS and optionally inspect traffic with `WAF`
- It is commonly used as the secure entry point for web applications

This section covers `Azure Front Door`, the global entry service used to route, accelerate, and protect web applications at the edge.

### *Azure Front Door*

`Azure Front Door` is a global Layer 7 service.

It sits at the Microsoft edge and routes user traffic to the best backend based on performance, health, and routing rules.

Unlike `Application Gateway`, which usually protects and routes traffic within one region or one application environment, `Front Door` works at the global level.

<Aside type="note">
`Azure Front Door` is often used when an application must serve users from multiple regions with low latency and high global availability.
</Aside>

### *What Front Door Does*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Global Routing" icon="document">
    Routes users to the closest or healthiest backend endpoint across regions.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Acceleration" icon="setting">
    Improves performance by using Microsoft's global edge network to bring traffic onto the backbone quickly.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Security" icon="warning">
    Can protect public applications with web application firewall features and centralized edge policies.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Key Features*

| Feature | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Global Load Balancing | Direct traffic across multiple regions or backend services |
| Health Probes | Detect unhealthy backends and stop sending traffic to them |
| SSL Offload | Terminate TLS at the edge |
| URL Routing | Route requests based on path or domain |
| Web Application Firewall | Protect against common web attacks |

### *How It Works*

`Azure Front Door` acts as the first global entry point for users.

It can route traffic to:

- `App Service`
- `Application Gateway`
- public endpoints
- multi-region web applications

### *Traffic Flow*

<Steps>
1. A user connects to the global `Front Door` endpoint.
2. Front Door evaluates routing rules, health, and backend priority.
3. Traffic is sent across Microsoft's global edge network.
4. The request reaches the selected backend in the best available region.
5. If one backend becomes unhealthy, traffic is redirected automatically.
</Steps>

### *Front Door Vs. Application Gateway*

| Service | Scope | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Application Gateway` | Regional | Web traffic routing and `WAF` inside one region or environment |
| `Azure Front Door` | Global | Multi-region applications, global failover, edge acceleration |

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Multi-Region Apps" icon="document">
    Direct users to the nearest or healthiest deployment across multiple Azure regions.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Global Failover" icon="warning">
    Redirect traffic automatically when one region becomes unavailable.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Edge Security" icon="setting">
    Apply centralized `WAF` policies and TLS handling before traffic reaches backend applications.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Summary*

- `Azure Front Door` is a global Layer 7 routing service
- It improves performance by routing traffic through Microsoft's edge network
- It supports global failover and multi-region application design
- It can provide `WAF` and TLS handling at the edge
- It complements regional services such as `Application Gateway`

This section covers `Azure DNS`, the Azure service used to host and manage domain name resolution.

### *Azure DNS*

`DNS` translates human-readable names such as `www.example.com` into IP addresses that computers can use.

`Azure DNS` is the Microsoft-managed service used to host DNS zones and records in Azure.

It is highly available, globally distributed, and integrated with the Azure platform.

<Aside type="note">
`Azure DNS` does not replace the DNS protocol. It provides managed hosting for your DNS zones and records.
</Aside>

### *DNS Zones*

A `DNS Zone` is the container for DNS records for a specific domain.

Examples:

- `example.com`
- `internal.corp.local`
- `myapp.contoso.com`

Inside the zone, you define the records that tell clients where services are located.

### *Common Record Types*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="A Record" icon="document">
    Maps a name to an IPv4 address.
  </Card>

  <Card title="CNAME Record" icon="setting">
    Maps one name to another DNS name.
  </Card>

  <Card title="MX Record" icon="warning">
    Defines the mail server responsible for a domain.
  </Card>

  <Card title="TXT Record" icon="database">
    Stores text-based values often used for verification, SPF, or configuration.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Public And Private DNS*

Azure supports both public and private DNS scenarios.

| Type | Use Case |
| --- | --- |
| Public DNS Zone | Resolve names from the public internet |
| Private DNS Zone | Resolve names only inside Azure VNets or connected private networks |

`Private DNS` is commonly used for internal applications, private endpoints, and hybrid networking.

### *How Azure DNS Works*

<Steps>
1. Create a DNS zone in Azure.
2. Add records such as `A`, `CNAME`, or `MX`.
3. If the zone is public, update the domain registrar to use the Azure name servers.
4. DNS clients query the zone.
5. Azure returns the matching record response.
</Steps>

### *Private DNS Zones*

`Private DNS Zones` are designed for internal name resolution.

They are useful when resources should be reachable by name without exposing them publicly.

Common examples include:

- internal applications in a `VNet`
- private database endpoints
- `Private Link` integrations

A private DNS zone can be linked to one or more VNets so resources in those networks can resolve the internal names.

### *Typical Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Public Websites" icon="document">
    Host DNS records for websites, APIs, and public-facing applications.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Private Applications" icon="database">
    Resolve internal service names inside VNets and private environments.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Service Integration" icon="setting">
    Support Azure services such as `Private Endpoint` with private DNS resolution.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Azure DNS Vs. Private DNS*

| Service | Scope | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Azure DNS` | Public internet | Public domains and internet-facing applications |
| `Azure Private DNS` | Internal networks | Private applications and internal service discovery |

### *Summary*

- `Azure DNS` hosts and manages DNS zones and records
- A `DNS Zone` contains records for a domain
- Azure supports both public and private DNS
- `Private DNS` is used for internal name resolution
- Azure DNS is commonly used with websites, APIs, and private endpoints

This section covers `Azure Private Link`, the Azure service used to access platform services and private applications through private network connectivity.

### *Azure Private Link*

`Azure Private Link` allows an Azure service to be accessed through a private IP address inside your `Virtual Network`.

Instead of reaching a service over the public internet, traffic stays on the private Azure network.

This is commonly used to access services such as:

- `Azure Storage`
- `Azure SQL`
- `Key Vault`
- privately exposed custom services

<Aside type="note">
`Private Link` is one of the main Azure services for reducing public exposure and building zero-trust style network architectures.
</Aside>

### *Private Endpoint*

The core component of `Private Link` is the `Private Endpoint`.

A `Private Endpoint` is a network interface inside your subnet that gets a private IP address and maps it to a specific Azure service.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Private IP" icon="document">
    The service becomes reachable through an IP address inside your own VNet.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Service Mapping" icon="setting">
    The private endpoint is linked to a specific Azure service resource.
  </Card>

  <Card title="No Public Exposure" icon="warning">
    Access can stay entirely on private connectivity without requiring public internet routing.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Why Use Private Link*

| Benefit | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Private Access | Access services over a private IP instead of a public endpoint |
| Reduced Exposure | Sensitive services do not need to be reachable from the internet |
| Compliance | Helps meet security and regulatory requirements |
| Better Isolation | Limits access paths to approved private networks |

### *Private Link Vs. Service Endpoints*

These services are related but solve different problems.

| Service | Main Idea |
| --- | --- |
| `Service Endpoints` | Extend VNet identity to an Azure service while the service still uses a public endpoint |
| `Private Link` | Gives the service a private IP inside the VNet |

`Private Link` is generally considered the more private and more secure option.

### *DNS And Private Link*

`Private Link` usually works together with `Private DNS`.

Without private DNS integration, applications may still resolve the public name of a service instead of the private endpoint.

This is why Azure commonly creates or links a `Private DNS Zone` when a private endpoint is deployed.

### *Typical Flow*

<Steps>
1. Create a `Private Endpoint` in a subnet.
2. Link it to a supported Azure service such as `Key Vault` or `Storage`.
3. Assign a private IP address inside the VNet.
4. Configure `Private DNS` so the service name resolves to the private IP.
5. Access the service privately from resources inside the VNet or connected networks.
</Steps>

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Private Storage Access" icon="document">
    Access storage accounts without exposing them to the public internet.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Private Database Access" icon="database">
    Connect privately to services such as `Azure SQL` from internal workloads.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Secure Platform Services" icon="warning">
    Reach sensitive Azure services such as `Key Vault` through private networking only.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Summary*

- `Private Link` gives Azure services private connectivity through a `Private Endpoint`
- The service becomes reachable through a private IP inside the VNet
- It is commonly used to reduce public exposure and improve security
- It is often combined with `Private DNS`
- It is more isolated than using `Service Endpoints`

This section covers `Azure NAT Gateway`, the Azure service used to provide controlled and scalable outbound internet access for resources in a virtual network.

### *Azure NAT Gateway*

`Azure NAT Gateway` is used when private resources inside a `VNet` need outbound internet access without exposing themselves to inbound public access.

It provides outbound-only connectivity.

This means resources such as virtual machines or containers can reach the internet, but the internet cannot directly initiate inbound connections back to them through the NAT gateway.

<Aside type="note">
`NAT Gateway` is commonly used when workloads in private subnets must access external services such as package repositories, APIs, or update servers.
</Aside>

### *Why Use NAT Gateway*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Outbound Only" icon="document">
    Enables internet access for private resources without giving them public IP addresses.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Stable Public IP" icon="setting">
    Outbound traffic uses one or more defined public IP addresses, making egress identity predictable.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Scalable SNAT" icon="warning">
    Provides more scalable source network address translation than relying on default outbound access.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *How NAT Gateway Works*

A `NAT Gateway` is associated with one or more subnets.

Resources in those subnets use the NAT gateway for outbound internet traffic.

The service translates private source IP addresses into the public IP address of the NAT gateway.

This lets multiple internal resources share controlled outbound connectivity.

### *Typical Flow*

<Steps>
1. Create a `NAT Gateway`.
2. Assign one or more public IP addresses or a public IP prefix.
3. Associate the NAT gateway with a subnet.
4. Deploy private resources into that subnet.
5. Outbound internet traffic uses the NAT gateway public IP for egress.
</Steps>

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Private VMs" icon="document">
    Allow virtual machines in private subnets to reach update services or external APIs.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Container Workloads" icon="database">
    Give containers outbound access without assigning public IPs to each workload.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Controlled Egress" icon="setting">
    Ensure outbound traffic leaves Azure through known public IP addresses for allowlisting.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *NAT Gateway Vs. Public IP*

| Option | Main Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Public IP on a VM | Direct internet exposure for that individual resource |
| `NAT Gateway` | Shared and controlled outbound-only connectivity for private subnet resources |

### *NAT Gateway Vs. Azure Firewall*

| Service | Best For |
| --- | --- |
| `NAT Gateway` | Simple outbound internet access with predictable egress IP |
| `Azure Firewall` | Centralized inspection, filtering, and policy-based traffic control |

### *Summary*

- `NAT Gateway` provides outbound-only internet access
- It is attached to a subnet, not to individual resources
- Private workloads can reach the internet without public IPs
- It provides stable and predictable egress IP addresses
- It is ideal for controlled outbound connectivity from private subnets

This section covers `Azure VPN Gateway`, the Azure service used to create encrypted tunnels between Azure and remote networks or individual clients.

### *Azure VPN Gateway*

`Azure VPN Gateway` is the managed Azure service used to connect a `Virtual Network` to:

- remote users
- branch offices
- on-premises datacenters

It creates encrypted tunnels over the public internet so traffic can move securely between Azure and external networks.

<Aside type="note">
`VPN Gateway` is a common hybrid connectivity option when an organization needs secure communication with Azure but does not require a dedicated private circuit like `ExpressRoute`.
</Aside>

### *Gateway Subnet*

To deploy a `VPN Gateway`, the VNet must contain a dedicated subnet named `GatewaySubnet`.

This subnet is reserved for the gateway service and should not host normal application resources.

### *Main VPN Types*

Azure VPN Gateway supports two main connection models.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Point-To-Site" icon="document">
    A single client device connects securely to Azure through an encrypted tunnel.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Site-To-Site" icon="database">
    An entire office or on-premises network connects to Azure through a persistent VPN tunnel.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Point-To-Site VPN*

`Point-to-Site (P2S)` is used when one user device needs access to Azure resources.

Common examples include:

- remote developers
- administrators working from home
- small teams without full office-to-cloud networking

The user connects from a laptop or workstation directly into Azure.

### *Site-To-Site VPN*

`Site-to-Site (S2S)` is used when an entire on-premises network must connect to Azure.

This allows office systems and Azure resources to communicate as if they were part of a larger connected environment.

It is commonly used by:

- small and medium businesses
- branch offices
- hybrid cloud environments

### *How It Works*

<Steps>
1. Create a `GatewaySubnet` inside the VNet.
2. Deploy the `VPN Gateway` resource.
3. Define the remote network or client configuration.
4. Establish the encrypted tunnel over the internet.
5. Exchange traffic securely between Azure and the remote side.
</Steps>

### *VPN Gateway Vs. ExpressRoute*

| Service | Connectivity Type | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VPN Gateway` | Encrypted tunnel over the public internet | Flexible and lower-cost hybrid connectivity |
| `ExpressRoute` | Dedicated private connection | High-bandwidth, low-latency enterprise connectivity |

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Remote Access" icon="document">
    Allow individual users to connect securely to Azure from their own devices.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Hybrid Networking" icon="setting">
    Connect on-premises offices or datacenters to Azure VNets.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Backup Connectivity" icon="warning">
    Use VPN as a backup or secondary path for hybrid connectivity designs.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Summary*

- `VPN Gateway` creates encrypted tunnels between Azure and remote networks or users
- It requires a dedicated subnet named `GatewaySubnet`
- `Point-to-Site` connects individual devices
- `Site-to-Site` connects entire networks
- It is a common hybrid connectivity solution when `ExpressRoute` is not required

This section covers `Azure ExpressRoute`, the Azure service used to create dedicated private connectivity between on-premises infrastructure and Azure.

### *Azure ExpressRoute*

`Azure ExpressRoute` provides a private, dedicated connection between your datacenter or network provider and Azure.

Unlike `VPN Gateway`, ExpressRoute does not use the public internet for traffic transport.

This makes it suitable for environments that need:

- lower latency
- more predictable performance
- higher bandwidth
- stronger network isolation

<Aside type="note">
`ExpressRoute` is commonly used by large enterprises that require private hybrid connectivity with more consistency than internet-based VPN connections.
</Aside>

### *Why Use ExpressRoute*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Private Connectivity" icon="document">
    Traffic does not traverse the public internet and stays on private network paths.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Predictable Performance" icon="setting">
    Provides more stable bandwidth and lower latency than internet-based connectivity.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Enterprise Scale" icon="warning">
    Designed for large organizations with demanding hybrid networking requirements.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *Main Characteristics*

`ExpressRoute` is often chosen when hybrid connectivity must support critical production workloads.

Typical goals include:

- private access to Azure services
- large-scale datacenter integration
- regulatory or compliance-driven network isolation
- resilient hybrid architecture

### *How It Works*

<Steps>
1. Establish a connection with an approved connectivity provider or exchange location.
2. Create an `ExpressRoute` circuit in Azure.
3. Link the circuit to one or more virtual networks through an `ExpressRoute Gateway`.
4. Route private traffic between the on-premises environment and Azure.
5. Use the connection for hybrid applications, data transfer, and private service access.
</Steps>

### *ExpressRoute Vs. VPN Gateway*

| Service | Connectivity Type | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VPN Gateway` | Encrypted tunnel over the public internet | Flexible and lower-cost hybrid connectivity |
| `ExpressRoute` | Dedicated private connection | Enterprise-grade hybrid networking with predictable performance |

### *Common Use Cases*

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Datacenter Extension" icon="document">
    Extend on-premises networks into Azure for hybrid infrastructure designs.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Critical Workloads" icon="database">
    Support production applications that need more stable and predictable connectivity.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Compliance Needs" icon="warning">
    Use private connectivity to support environments with strict regulatory or security requirements.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

### *ExpressRoute Gateway*

To connect a VNet to an ExpressRoute circuit, Azure uses an `ExpressRoute Gateway`.

This gateway is deployed inside the VNet and allows traffic from Azure workloads to flow through the private circuit.

### *Summary*

- `ExpressRoute` provides private dedicated connectivity to Azure
- It does not rely on the public internet for traffic transport
- It is designed for enterprise hybrid networking
- It offers more predictable performance than `VPN Gateway`
- It is commonly used for critical workloads, datacenter extension, and compliance-sensitive environments
